property_summary: The contract's owner() should always return the stored owner address (_owner) after initialization; the mutant returns address(0) instead, so for some fuzzed initialOwner the returned value will differ.

For any deployed and initialized contract C, owner() must return the stored owner address (non-zero when initialized by __Ownable_init); the mutant returns address(0) instead, violating this for some initialized owner addresses.

After initialize(...) is called, owner() must return the stored owner address (the caller that initialized); the mutant always returns address(0) so for some fuzzed initializer addresses the returned owner differs and the property is violated.

After initialize(...) is called by any caller, the reference contract's owner() returns that initializer address (nonzero), whereas the mutant always returns address(0), so for some fuzzed initializer addresses the returned owner differs.

For any address initializer, after calling initialize(...) on C the public owner() getter must return the stored owner (the initializer); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this rule for some initializer addresses (the fuzzer will find one).

For any caller address x, the correct contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (not the caller), whereas the mutant wrongly returns msg.sender for some callers, so owner() must not equal the caller for all callers (i.e., there exists a caller where owner() != caller), which the mutant will violate by returning caller.

For any caller address, the correct contract's owner() returns the stored owner() value (the deployer set in initialize/__Ownable_init), whereas the mutant returns tx.origin which can differ for calls made via other senders — so there exists a caller address for which owner() differs between reference and mutant.

For every caller (msg.sender) calling owner(), the reference contract returns the stored _owner (the deployer after initialization); the mutant returns tx.origin which differs when the call is proxied through another contract, so calling owner() through an intermediary contract yields different results.

For any caller address that directly calls C.owner(), the reference returns the stored owner (deployer) while the mutant may return a different address when the call originates via a proxy contract (tx.origin ≠ stored owner); thus the general rule: owner() return value is invariant to call routing — it always equals the stored owner, but mutant breaks this when invoked through an intermediate contract (so there exists an intermediary address for which returned owner differs).

For every caller (including EOAs), C.owner() always returns the stored owner address (the deployer set during initialization); the mutant returns tx.origin instead, so when an EOA calls C.owner() via an intermediate contract (so msg.sender != tx.origin), the returned value differs and the rule is violated.

For every caller (including calls proxied through other contracts), the genuine contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the deployer set during initialization); the mutant that returns tx.origin can differ when owner() is invoked via a proxy contract whose msg.sender ≠ tx.origin, so there exist proxy addresses that cause owner() to return a different value.

For every call, the contract's owner() returns the externally stored owner address (the Ownable _owner) — the mutant returns address(this) instead, so there exist inputs where owner()'s returned address differs (i.e., owner() must equal the contract's stored owner rather than address(this)).

For every input the reference contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the deployer), i.e. owner() != address(this) for contracts where the stored owner is not the contract itself; the mutant returning address(this) breaks this by making owner() equal address(this) for those cases.

For every deployer address X, the correct contract's owner() returns X (the stored owner), whereas the mutant sometimes returns address(this) causing owner() == address(c) for some deployers — the property: owner() != address(c) for any deployer that is not the contract itself; the mutant violates this for those deployers.

For any deployer address D, the correct contract's owner() returns D (the externally stored owner set at initialization), so owner() equals the deployer address; the mutant returns address(this) instead, so there exist deployer addresses where owner() != deployer, breaking the rule owner() == deployer for those deployers.

For every deployment sender (deployer) D, the reference contract's owner() returns D (the stored owner set during initialization); the mutant that returns address(this) will for some deployers return address(c) != D, violating this rule.

Invariant: calling transferOwnership(newOwner) as the current owner must revert if newOwner is the zero address; the mutant removes that check allowing transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed and thus changes owner to zero for some input (newOwner == address(0)).

For any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) by the current owner must revert if newOwner == address(0); the mutant removes this require allowing transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed, so the reference always reverts for zero address while the mutant does not.

For any caller who is the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) always reverts if newOwner == address(0) (reference enforces non-zero newOwner); the mutant removes that check so calling transferOwnership(address(0)) by the owner may succeed — the test ensures the reference always reverts for zero newOwner while the mutant can succeed for that input.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) MUST revert when newOwner is the zero address (reference enforces this); the mutant removed that check so calling transferOwnership(address(0)) by the owner can succeed and change owner to zero, violating the rule.

For any caller equal to the current owner and any candidate newOwner address, the reference C always reverts when newOwner == address(0) (it forbids transferring ownership to the zero address); the mutant removes that require and therefore allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed for some input, violating this rule.

For any non-zero newOwner address, transferOwnership succeeds on the reference contract (owner becomes newOwner); the mutant forbids non-zero newOwner and thus reverts for some non-zero addresses, violating this property.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (does not revert) and updates owner to newOwner; the mutant inverts the require and thus will revert for non-zero newOwner values breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any caller that is the contract owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference always returns (does not revert) and updates owner() to newOwner; the mutant inverts the require and will revert for many non-zero newOwner addresses, thus violating this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) does not revert on the reference C (and sets owner() to newOwner); the mutant inverts the require and will revert for many non-zero newOwner addresses, so there exists fuzzed newOwner values for which transferOwnership reverts under the mutant but not under the reference.

For any caller that is the current owner and for any newOwner address, the reference contract allows transferOwnership(newOwner) to succeed (does not revert) and sets owner() to newOwner; the mutant inverts the require to only permit the zero address, causing calls with non-zero newOwner to revert and thus violating this property for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract only succeeds when the caller is the current owner and results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant inverts onlyOwner so a non-owner can call transferOwnership and the owner() after the call can differ (i.e. the call behavior/ownership change differs for some callers).

Rule: Only the contract owner can successfully call transferOwnership (calls from non-owners revert); the mutant removing the onlyOwner guard allows non-owners to change owner and thus sometimes succeeds where the reference reverts.

For every input the correct contract returns paused() == _paused (i.e., paused() reflects the internal paused flag), whereas the mutant returns the negation for some inputs, so paused() must equal the internal flag in the reference but differs in the mutant.

For every caller/address the reference contract's paused() returns the stored paused flag (so it can be false after initialization), whereas the mutant always returns true; thus there exists calls (e.g., immediately after initialize where paused is false) for which reference.paused() == false but mutant.paused() == true.

For every deployment and initialization, the reference contract's paused() can return false (reflecting the stored _paused flag) for some inputs (e.g., after initialize/unpause) while the mutant always returns true; the property: there exists an input sequence where paused() == false on the reference — the mutant violates this by always returning true.

For any account and after initialization the reference contract can report paused() == false (unpaused) for some caller sequences, while the mutant always returns true; the property asserts that immediately after initialize() the contract reports paused() == false (which the mutant breaks).

For every C instance, after calling initialize(...) with a valid nonzero keeper and valid addresses, paused() is false (contract starts unpaused); the mutant that forces paused() to always return true violates this (some inputs will make reference.paused() == false while mutant.paused() == true).

For any address input `actor`, calling the public view `paused()` on the correct contract can return either true or false depending on state, and specifically there exist fuzzed inputs (an address used as keeper in initialize) for which after initialize(...) the reference returns false while the mutant that forces paused() to always return true will return true, so assert that paused() is false after initialize with a nonzero keeper address.

For any caller, C.paused() always returns the stored _paused flag (reflecting pause state); the mutant returns false regardless, so there exist inputs where paused() differs (e.g., after _pause() is called).

For any account and any sequence, after calling c.pauseDeposit() (which calls _pause via onlyKeeper) the reference returns paused() == true, but the mutant's paused() always returns false so this will differ for inputs where pauseDeposit can be invoked (i.e. when called by the keeper).

For every keeper address k, after initialize is called with k as keeper and that keeper calls pauseDeposit(), the reference contract's paused() returns true, while the mutant (which forces paused() to always return false) will return false for at least some keeper addresses (so paused() differs); thus: for any keeper address the reference yields paused()==true after pauseDeposit() called by keeper, but the mutant yields paused()==false for some inputs.

For any keeper address K and any nonzero keeper caller setup, if the keeper calls pauseDeposit() the reference contract's paused() returns true, whereas the mutant that forces paused() to always return false will return false — so after a keeper-triggered pause, paused()==true always holds in the reference but not in the mutant for some inputs.

For any keeper address K and any keeper-invokable call that causes the contract to pause (pauseDeposit called by K), the reference contract's paused() returns true afterwards for all inputs; the mutant always returns false so there exist inputs (keeper K calling pauseDeposit) where paused() differs and the mutant breaks this rule.

For any caller address provided by the owner to setKeeper, the contract's keeper getter equals the provided address after the call; the mutant assigns keeper = address(0) instead, violating this for many inputs.

For any nonzero address passed to setKeeper by the owner, the correct contract sets keeper() to that address; the mutant incorrectly sets keeper() to address(0), so there exist inputs (any nonzero address) where keeper() differs after the call.

For any address x passed to setKeeper by the contract owner, the correct contract sets keeper() == x after the call; the mutant sets keeper() == address(0) for many x (e.g., any nonzero x), so the property is violated for those inputs.

For any address k provided by the contract owner to setKeeper(k), the correct contract sets keeper() == k after the call; the mutant sets keeper() == address(0) for many k, so there exist inputs where keeper() differs.

For any address k supplied by the owner to setKeeper(k), the reference contract sets keeper() == k after the call; the mutant sets keeper() == address(0) for many k, so there exist inputs where keeper() differs.

For any caller `owner` and any address `newKeeper`, calling setKeeper(newKeeper) sets c.keeper() equal to the provided newKeeper (the reference emits event with new value); the mutant emits the old value instead and thus after the call c.keeper() will not match the provided newKeeper for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any nonzero address newKeeper, calling setKeeper(newKeeper) results in c.keeper() == newKeeper (reference emits event with new value and assigns it); the mutant emits the old keeper in the event (and its assignment causes keeper to differ from the provided newKeeper for some inputs), so asserting the stored keeper equals the provided newKeeper distinguishes them.

For any caller who is the owner and any address newKeeper, after calling setKeeper(newKeeper) the contract's keeper() getter returns exactly the provided newKeeper; the mutant emits the old keeper value in the event (and in the faulty variant this results in keeper() not equaling the provided newKeeper for some inputs).

For any caller that is the owner and any address newKeeper, after calling setKeeper(newKeeper) the contract's keeper() getter returns the provided newKeeper; the mutant emits the old keeper value instead and thus its stored keeper may differ from the provided newKeeper for some input.
